title: Saying No as a Developer Without Becoming the Difficult One
summary: Every yes to a late request gets paid for somehow. How to name the trade-off, tell urgent from loud, offer a smaller shape and say no while there is still time to adjust.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
It's 5:40 p.m. The release goes out tomorrow morning, the checklist is mostly green, and people are starting to close tabs. Then a message pops up: "Can we also add a CSV export to this page before tomorrow? It's just one button."

It's never just one button. There's the query behind it, the permission check (should support staff see every customer's phone number?), Vietnamese characters that turn to garbage when Excel opens a UTF-8 file without a BOM, and the test you'd normally write. Everyone's tired, everyone wants to be helpful, and "sure, no problem" is sitting right there on your keyboard.

Developers are trained to find a way. We like solving things, and on a lot of teams the person who says yes gets called a team player while the person who pauses gets called slow. So we take one more task, then one more exception, then one more urgent fix, until the plan no longer tells the truth about time or quality. This post is about saying no in a way that keeps you useful, and keeps your yes worth something.

Every yes spends something

A yes to the CSV button gets paid for somehow. Maybe with tests you skip. Maybe with your evening. Maybe with a bug report next week when a customer opens the file and sees boxes instead of names. The cost doesn't vanish because nobody wrote it down. It just lands on someone later, usually you.

Some of that cost lands on people, too. In a lab experiment, Gloria Mark and colleagues at UC Irvine had people answer email with and without interruptions (The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress, CHI 2008). The surprise: interrupted people finished faster, with no drop in quality. But they paid for it with "more stress, higher frustration, time pressure and effort." Teams that pile on late requests often look fine on the dashboard. The bill shows up in how worn out everyone feels.

Say the price, and let them choose

A flat "no" makes you the obstacle. Spell out the trade-off instead, and you're making the decision together. Try "yes, if" sentences:

  • "Yes, if we move the reporting fix to next sprint."
  • "Yes, if we ship it to admins only for now and skip the permission work."
  • "I can hack a prototype tonight. I can't make it production-safe by tomorrow."

You're putting the cost on the table, so the person asking can decide whether it's worth it. Often they'll say "oh, then next week is fine." They didn't know the price until you said it.

Basecamp's Shape Up gives this a useful frame. Instead of estimating how long a feature takes, set an "appetite": how much time is this worth to us? Their rule is fixed time, variable scope, which they call "key to successfully defining and shipping projects." When the date can't move, the scope has to. Asking "how much is this worth?" before "how long will it take?" makes trimming scope feel normal, and nobody hears it as you refusing to work.

Is it urgent, or does it just feel urgent?

In a 1954 speech, President Eisenhower quoted an unnamed former college president: "I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent" (Address at the World Council of Churches). That's too absolute for software. Production being down is both. But the split is handy.

Some work really is urgent: production is down, a customer is blocked, a legal deadline moved, a security hole is open. Plenty of other work only feels urgent because someone just noticed it, or a meeting ran hot, or waiting is uncomfortable. You don't need to wave that pressure away. Just help name it with one question: "What happens if this ships Thursday instead of tomorrow?" If the answer is "nothing much," you've got your answer.

Offer another shape

A good no usually comes with an alternative. Keep the goal, change the shape:

  • "Not in this release, but I'll write up the proper approach and an estimate by Friday."
  • "Not as a one-off exception for this customer. Let's fix the underlying rule next sprint."
  • "Not with this API shape. Here's a smaller version that doesn't lock us in."

For raw ideas that show up mid-sprint, Shape Up suggests a default reply: "Interesting. Maybe some day." It's a soft no that keeps the idea alive without committing anyone to it. The same chapter warns that saying yes to everything leaves you with a pile of work that only grows.

Early, specific, no drama

The best no comes early, says exactly what's wrong and doesn't come with a sigh. Early, because a no on release morning feels like a betrayal even when you're right, and every day earlier leaves the team more options. Specific, because "I don't feel good about this" sounds like taste, while "this export has no permission check, so support could download every customer's phone number" sounds like a fact. And keep the drama out, because panic makes people defend their idea and stop hearing yours.

This gets harder early in your career. It's easy to assume the senior engineer, the PM or the manager sees the full picture. Sometimes they do. Often they don't see the implementation cost, because you're the one inside that code. Your job isn't to overrule anyone. It's to add the facts you're closest to.

Over time, something good happens. People learn that when you say yes, you mean it, because they've heard you say "yes, if" and "not this week." Your yes becomes a commitment people can plan around. If the request is a whole release that isn't ready, the culture series has a post on saying "not yet" to a release.

Try this week

  • Next time a late request comes in, reply with one "yes, if" sentence before you start coding.
  • Ask "what happens if this ships Thursday instead?" at least once.
  • Ask for the appetite before you give an estimate: how much time is this worth?
  • Write down one thing you said yes to last month that cost more than anyone expected. Use it next time.

faqs.q: How do I say no to a feature request without sounding negative?
faqs.a: Name the trade-off and let the other person choose. "Yes, if we move the reporting fix to next sprint" or "yes, for admins only for now" puts the decision back on the table for both of you. Most people just didn't know the cost yet.

faqs.q: How can I tell if a request is really urgent?
faqs.a: Ask what happens if it ships a few days later. Production outages, blocked customers, legal deadlines and open security holes can't wait. If the honest answer is "nothing much," the request is loud rather than urgent.

faqs.q: When is the best time to push back on scope?
faqs.a: As early as you can. A no on release morning feels like a betrayal even when it's correct, while a no a week earlier leaves the team room to cut scope, move the date or change the approach.
